title: Compute choices, cost and FinOps reasoning
summary: Answer a sponsor's cost question with drivers in their own units, compute chosen from each workload's pattern, idle, startup, queue and quota evidence, attribution from the billable usage table, unit costs with a guard, and a low, base and high sensitivity table.
objectives: List a workload's cost drivers in their own units and periods and choose compute for each workload from its pattern.
Separate idle, startup and queue time, trace a failed launch to a cloud quota, and attribute usage with tags and the billable usage system table.
Compute unit economics with a zero-count guard, refuse sums across units, and build a low, base and high sensitivity table with labelled hypothetical rates.

questions.prompt: At 07:31 on a month-end morning, dashboard users wait ten seconds, yet each query executes in about five. Which evidence separates the waiting from the executing before anyone resizes the warehouse?

options.text: Per-query timings that record provisioning and at-capacity waits apart from compilation and execution.
options.rationale: Correct: those fields show whether time went to starting compute, to a full warehouse or to the query itself, which decides the fix.

options.text: The warehouse's size label and its cluster count settings.
options.rationale: Settings say what capacity was allowed, not where the ten seconds went; they cannot separate waiting from executing.

options.text: The month's budget total for the workspace.
options.rationale: A monthly spend figure carries no per-query timing, so it cannot tell a queue from a slow query.

options.text: The custom_tags column on the billable usage rows.
options.rationale: Tags attribute usage to owners; they carry no latency and say nothing about why a query waited.

questions.prompt: A draft worksheet adds 300 DBU, 120 instance-hours and 500 GB-month and reports a total of 920. What should the cost model do with this line?

options.text: Refuse the sum, price each quantity with its own labelled rate, then add the amounts in one currency per month.
options.rationale: Correct: only amounts in one currency and one period can be added, and each billing unit needs its own rate first.

options.text: Accept 920 as total usage units, since each quantity was measured.
options.rationale: Each number was measured in a different unit, so their sum has no unit, no currency and no meaning.

options.text: Average the three quantities to get a representative usage figure.
options.rationale: Averaging unlike units is as meaningless as adding them; an average of DBUs and GB-months is not a quantity of anything.

options.text: Convert instance-hours to DBUs one for one, then add everything as DBUs.
options.rationale: No fixed one-to-one conversion exists; DBUs per hour depend on the compute used, and storage is a different driver altogether.

cards.prompt: A sponsor asks what the pilot will cost. Why is a single number the wrong first answer?
cards.answer: Because the cost comes from several drivers in different units and periods, each with its own owner and uncertainty.
cards.explanation: Compute time, platform usage, storage, data movement, operations effort and a one-off migration are counted in instance-hours, DBUs, GB-months, GB, hours per week and hours once. Listing them first shows which ones a decision moves and which input is least known before any total is quoted.

cards.prompt: Which compute class fits a scheduled batch that is idle between runs, and why?
cards.answer: Job compute created for each run, because it exists only while the run does and terminates when it completes.
cards.explanation: An always-on cluster would pay for the idle hours between runs and share its capacity with interactive users. Job compute removes the idle time at the price of one startup per run, and serverless jobs remove the instance provisioning where the workspace allows them.

cards.prompt: An all-purpose cluster runs from 08:00 to 18:00 and is busy for two hours. What is its utilization, and which setting removes the paid idle hours?
cards.answer: Twenty percent, and auto-termination ends the cluster after a set number of idle minutes.
cards.explanation: Utilization is useful work divided by running time over one period, here 2 ÷ 10. Without auto-termination an all-purpose cluster runs until someone stops it, so the eight idle hours are paid; a compute policy can require auto-termination for everyone who creates interactive compute.

cards.prompt: Predict which run pays the larger share of its running time for a three-minute startup: a six-minute job or a sixty-minute job.
cards.answer: The six-minute job, where startup is a third of the running time against under five percent for the long job.
cards.explanation: Startup is paid once per start whatever the run length: 3 ÷ 9 = 33.3 percent against 3 ÷ 63 = 4.8 percent. Splitting work into many short jobs multiplies startups, which is why batching, pools or serverless matter most for short, frequent work.

cards.prompt: Dashboard users wait ten seconds at 07:31 but each query executes in five. Which change addresses the wait?
cards.answer: More concurrent capacity, such as a higher maximum cluster count, or moving the arrivals; not a rewritten query.
cards.explanation: The extra five seconds are waiting at capacity, which query timings record apart from execution. Clusters serve concurrent queries while a larger size helps queries that spill, so resizing for a queue buys the wrong capacity; staggering refreshes after the nightly job can remove the peak instead.

cards.prompt: A scheduled job never started and produced no usage rows. Where should you look first?
cards.answer: At the launch's termination reason, such as a cloud quota or capacity failure, before any usage evidence.
cards.explanation: Classic compute launches instances in the customer's cloud account, which can refuse them. AWS_RESOURCE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED points at the account's limit and whatever else holds it; AWS_INSUFFICIENT_INSTANCE_CAPACITY_FAILURE points at the zone's supply, where a retry or an alternate node type helps.

cards.prompt: Why can't you fix last month's attribution by tagging the exploration cluster today?
cards.answer: Usage rows keep the tags the resource had when the usage happened, so new tags attribute only future usage.
cards.explanation: Tags are written into each billable usage row as it is recorded. Old rows can still be grouped by the cluster identifier in their metadata and allocated by a documented rule, but that is an analyst's allocation; the lasting fix is a policy that requires tags at creation.

cards.prompt: Why must a sum over the billable usage table include retraction and restatement rows?
cards.answer: Because corrections arrive as new rows that negate and replace the original, so only the full signed sum is right.
cards.explanation: A wrong original row is not edited in place: a retraction row cancels it and a restatement row carries the corrected quantity. Filtering to original rows keeps the error, while summing every record type gives the corrected usage, as in 5.0 − 5.0 + 4.5 = 4.5 DBU.

cards.prompt: What belongs in the numerator of a cost per run, and what should a month with no runs return?
cards.answer: Only the drivers the runs cause, and unknown with a zero-denominator reason when no run happened.
cards.explanation: Fixed costs such as operations effort make a fully loaded ratio that falls whenever runs rise, so they are reported separately and labelled. A zero count has no cost per run: printing 0.00 would claim the work was free, and an exception would lose the rest of the report.

cards.prompt: Spot the error in the worksheet line '300 DBU + 120 instance-hours + 500 GB-month = 920'.
cards.answer: It adds three different billing units, so the 920 has no unit, no currency and no meaning.
cards.explanation: Each quantity must be priced with its own labelled rate and restated to one period first: 150.00 + 48.00 + 10.00 = 208.00 hypothetical USD per month. Only amounts in one currency and one period can be added or compared.

cards.prompt: In Cinderline's worksheet, which driver has the largest swing, and what should the sponsor measure first?
cards.answer: Operations effort, which swings the month by 1,170.00 hypothetical USD, so logged operations hours come first.
cards.explanation: Platform usage swings only 150.00 and compute time 48.00. A sensitivity table exists to show where the uncertainty lives; here it is people's hours, so tuning DBUs first would work the smaller lever while the widest input stays unmeasured.

cards.prompt: A budget alert emailed the data lead at 80 percent. Did anything stop the idle cluster?
cards.answer: No; an email alert informs people, while policies, auto-termination or a verified blocking action change what runs.
cards.explanation: The budget measured cumulative monthly spend and notified its recipients. The cluster kept running because no policy had required auto-termination. The current budget API lists a block-usage action type, so check the documentation for what it covers before depending on it.

cards.prompt: Why is a configuration observed in only one run left out of the cost ranking?
cards.answer: Because one observation has no spread, so it cannot show whether its cost or speed is typical.
cards.explanation: The experiment ranks configurations with at least three runs by median cost per unit of work and checks whether the ranges overlap. xlarge's single run at 4.00 per 1,000 items may be unusual in either direction, so the honest next step is to repeat it.
